reference_title: Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements

sections.title: Purpose
sections.summary: This UFC documents the standard practice for improving the engineering properties of soils used for operating surfaces, pavement base/subbase courses, and subgrades by mixing in additives (lime, cement, bitumen, etc.). It applies to roads, airfields, and construction platforms with a stabilized surface layer.
sections.body: This UFC documents the standard practice for improving the engineering properties of soils used for operating surfaces, pavement base courses, subbase courses, and subgrades by the use of additives mixed into the soil to effect the desired improvement. It also provides criteria and guidance for the stabilization and modification of soils for pavements, operating surfaces, and construction platforms. This UFC is also applicable to roads, airfields, and construction platforms having a stabilized surface layer. These soil improvements consist of applying a chemical such as lime, cement, or bitumen to a layer of soil or aggregate that will be included within a pavement area. Stabilization or modification measures discussed herein are useful to limit expansive soil's ability to expand and contract due to changes in moisture content, increase the soil's shear strength to prevent or minimize pumping, or to bind soils or aggregates.
key_points: Documents standard practice for improving engineering properties of soils via additives (lime, cement, bitumen, etc.)
Covers pavement base/subbase courses, subgrades, and operating surfaces
Applicable to roads, airfields, and construction platforms with a stabilized surface layer
Goals: limit expansive-soil swell/shrink, increase shear strength to prevent pumping, or bind soils/aggregates
sections.applicability: Orientation to the document's overall purpose before applying additive-selection and design procedures.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Prescribes the appropriate additive type(s) for different soil types, procedures for determining design treatment level, and standard construction practices. Covers portland cement, lime, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash, bitumen, polymer, lime-cement, lime-bitumen, and geosynthetic fibers.
sections.body: This UFC prescribes the appropriate type(s) of additive to be used with different soil types, procedures for determining a design treatment level for each type of additive, and standard construction practices for incorporating the additive into the soil. This UFC provides criteria and guidance on stabilization or modification using portland cement, lime, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash, bitumen, polymer, lime-cement, lime-bitumen, or geo-synthetic fibers.
key_points: Prescribes appropriate additive type(s) by soil type
Covers determination of design treatment level per additive
Covers standard construction practices for incorporating additive into soil
Additives in scope: portland cement, lime, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash, bitumen, polymer, lime-cement, lime-bitumen, geosynthetic fibers
sections.applicability: Defines the boundaries of what stabilizer types and design/construction topics this UFC covers.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.summary: Soil stabilization and modification are optional; the installation, with the designers of record, decides whether to include it in the pavement design. When included, this UFC's requirements apply, dependent on each site's soil conditions.
sections.body: Soil stabilization and modification are optional. The installation, in conjunction with the designers of record, determines whether to include soil stabilization or modification in the pavement design. Apply the requirements in this UFC when soil stabilization or modification is included in the design. These requirements are dependent upon each individual site's soil conditions.
key_points: Soil stabilization/modification is an optional design decision, not mandatory
Installation and designers of record jointly decide whether to include it
When included, this UFC's requirements apply
Requirements are site-specific (dependent on individual site soil conditions)
sections.applicability: Clarifies that stabilization is a project decision; once chosen, the UFC's criteria become mandatory for that project.

sections.title: Uses of Stabilization/Modification
sections.summary: Pavement design assumes each layer achieves a specified structural quality. As a soil layer's quality increases, its ability to distribute load over a greater area increases, allowing a reduction in required thickness of the soil and surface layers above it.
sections.body: Pavement design is based on the premise that the specified structural quality will be achieved for each layer of material in the pavement system. Each layer resists shearing, avoids excessive deflections that cause cracking within the layer or in overlying layers, and prevents excessive permanent deformation. As the quality of a soil layer is increased, the ability of that layer to distribute the load over a greater area is increased so a reduction in the required thickness of the soil and surface layers is achieved.
key_points: Pavement design assumes each layer achieves a specified structural quality
Layers must resist shearing, avoid excessive deflection/cracking, and prevent permanent deformation
Higher soil-layer quality distributes load over a greater area
This enables reduced required thickness of soil and surface layers (see 1-4.2, Appendix A)
sections.applicability: Frames the three specific benefits (quality improvement, thickness reduction, operating surfaces) detailed in the child sections.

sections.title: Quality Improvement
sections.summary: Common improvements from stabilization/modification include better soil gradation, reduced plasticity index (PI) or swelling potential, and increased durability and strength. Stabilization may also provide a working platform for construction.
sections.body: The most common improvements achieved through stabilization/modification include better soil gradation, reduced plasticity index (PI) or swelling potential, and increased durability and strength. Stabilization may be used to provide a working platform for construction.
key_points: Better soil gradation
Reduced plasticity index (PI) or swelling potential
Increased durability and strength
Can provide a working platform for construction
sections.applicability: Applies when the design objective is improving in-place soil quality rather than primarily reducing pavement thickness.

sections.title: Thickness Reduction
sections.summary: Additives can improve a soil layer's strength enough to permit a reduction in design thickness versus an unstabilized/unbound material, provided gradation, strength, stability, and durability requirements are met. Appendix A gives worked examples.
sections.body: The strength of a soil layer can be improved through the use of additives to permit a reduction in design thickness of the stabilized material compared with an unstabilized or unbound material. Procedures for designing and evaluating pavements that include stabilized soils are presented in UFC 3-250-01, Paving Design for Roads and Parking Areas, UFC 3-250-03, Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements, and UFC 3-260-02, Pavement Design for Airfields. The design thickness of a base or subbase course can be reduced if the stabilized material meets the specified gradation, strength, stability, and durability requirements indicated in this UFC for the particular type of material. See Appendix A for examples of reducing design thickness when using stabilized materials.
key_points: Additive-improved strength permits reduced design thickness vs. unstabilized material
Pavement design/evaluation procedures with stabilized soils are in UFC 3-250-01, 3-250-03, and 3-260-02
Reduced thickness requires meeting this UFC's gradation, strength, stability, and durability requirements
Appendix A (Table A-1 equivalency factors) gives worked thickness-reduction examples
sections.applicability: Governing paragraph for the thickness-equivalency design procedure fully worked out in Appendix A.

sections.title: Operating Surfaces
sections.summary: Stabilized materials can construct operating surfaces, typically temporary construction platforms, roads, or airfields where poor soils exist and conventional pavements cannot be feasibly built; strength, durability, and construction criteria in this UFC apply.
sections.body: Stabilized materials can be used to construct operating surfaces. These cases are typically for temporary construction platforms, roads, or airfields where poor soils exist and conventional pavements cannot be feasibly constructed. For roads and airfields, adhere to the strength, durability, and construction criteria in this UFC.
key_points: Stabilized materials can construct operating surfaces directly (not just as a pavement layer)
Typical use case: temporary construction platforms, roads, or airfields over poor soils
Applies when conventional pavement construction is not feasible
This UFC's strength, durability, and construction criteria still apply
sections.applicability: Applies to temporary/expedient construction platforms and operating surfaces rather than permanent pavement structures.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.summary: Appendix B contains the list of acronyms and definitions used throughout this UFC, including the key distinction between 'modification' (property improvement without a major strength/durability gain) and 'stabilization' (a significant strength/durability increase).
sections.body: Appendix B contains a list of acronyms and definitions. This includes the key distinction, used throughout the UFC, between soil MODIFICATION (a stabilization process that improves a material property such as PI but does not, by design, result in a significant increase in strength and durability) and soil STABILIZATION (which does result in a significant strength and/or durability increase).
key_points: All acronyms and term definitions are consolidated in Appendix B
Key defined terms include Stabilization, Modification, Mechanical Stabilization, Additive Stabilization, Durability, Optimum Moisture Content, and Strength
sections.applicability: Pointer to Appendix B for terminology used throughout the document.

sections.title: References
sections.summary: Appendix C contains the list of references cited in this document. The referenced publication's date is not included; unless otherwise specified, the most recent edition applies.
sections.body: Appendix C contains a list of references used in this document. The publication date of the code or standard is not included in this document. Unless otherwise specified, the most recent edition of the referenced publication applies.
key_points: All references (DoD/UFC, AASHTO, ACI, ASTM) are consolidated in Appendix C
Publication dates are intentionally omitted from citations
Default rule: the most recent edition of a referenced publication applies unless otherwise specified
sections.applicability: Pointer to Appendix C for the full referenced-document list.
